comparisons.peer_topic: Intangible Asset Accounting and Impairment Methodology
comparisons.peer_summary: The company initially records intangible assets at cost or fair value upon acquisition, subsequently amortizing finite-lived assets over their estimated useful lives while testing indefinite-lived assets for annual impairment. Impairment assessments for both asset types are based on subjective inputs like forecasted cash flows and discount rates, with no subsequent reversal of recognized impairment losses permitted.
comparisons.comparison: Both Goldman Sachs (GS) and Morgan Stanley (MS) disclose the specific methodology for testing identifiable intangible assets for impairment, relying on undiscounted cash flow tests for recoverability. GS states that impairment is recognized if estimated undiscounted cash flows are less than the carrying value, and it recognized a specific $72 million write-down for the GM credit card program in 2024. MS provides a broader policy description for amortizable intangible assets, stating an impairment loss exists if the carrying amount is not recoverable (exceeding expected undiscounted cash flows) and exceeds its fair value. While GS highlights a specific realized loss event in 2024, MS details the accounting policy framework without citing a specific 2024 write-down amount in this excerpt.

sentences.text: An impairment is recognized if the estimated undiscounted cash flows relating to the asset or asset group is less than the corresponding carrying value.

During 2024, in connection with the planned transition of the GM credit card program to another issuer, we classified the GM credit card program to held for sale and recognized a $72 million write-down of identifiable intangible assets.

• For amortizable intangible assets, an impairment loss exists if the carrying amount of the intangible asset is not recoverable and exceeds its fair value. The carrying amount of the intangible asset is not recoverable if it exceeds the sum of the expected undiscounted cash flows.
